nameStory: Mountain tarweed gets its name from two key traits: it grows in mountainous areas and produces a sticky, tar-like resin that coats its stems and leaves. This gummy substance was once considered a nuisance to hikers and livestock, earning it the 'tarweed' moniker, though the plant isn't actually related to tar at all!
description: Mountain tarweed is a sturdy annual wildflower that belongs to the sunflower family. It typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a branched, upright stem covered in sticky hairs and resin. The plant produces small, yellow daisy-like flowers clustered at the tips of its branches. Its narrow leaves are arranged alternately along the stem and are also covered in the characteristic sticky coating.

idTips.label: Sticky coating
idTips.description: The entire plant feels noticeably sticky and gummy to the touch, with a tar-like resin that will cling to your fingers and clothes - this is the plant's signature feature

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow daisy-like flowers about half an inch across, clustered in tight groups at branch tips, each with 5-8 narrow petals surrounding a yellow center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that alternate up the stem, covered in sticky hairs that make them feel rough and gummy when touched

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant 1-3 feet tall with multiple branches from the base, creating a somewhat bushy appearance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Green to reddish stems densely covered in sticky, glandular hairs that give off a resinous smell when crushed

habitat: Mountain tarweed is extremely rare in New England, with only one confirmed observation in the region. It typically grows in dry, rocky slopes and open areas at higher elevations. When found, it prefers well-drained soils in areas with full sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring, producing small rosettes of sticky leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin flowering in mid to late summer, reaching their full height and producing the characteristic yellow blooms.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming into early fall, followed by seed production. The sticky coating becomes even more pronounced as the plant matures.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely after the first hard frost, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil.

funFact: The sticky resin produced by mountain tarweed was historically used by some Native American tribes as a natural glue for waterproofing baskets and repairing tools - essentially making the plant a living hardware store!
confusionNotes: Mountain tarweed might be confused with other small yellow wildflowers in the aster family, but the incredibly sticky, tar-like coating on all parts of the plant is unmistakable - no other New England wildflower will make your hands this gummy! Remember: if it's sticky like tar, you've found your tarweed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'mountain tarweed,' this plant is actually a western North American species that is extremely rare in New England - so rare that there's only been one confirmed sighting in the entire region. Any potential sighting should be carefully documented and reported to local botanists.
compareHints: Since mountain tarweed is the only Madia species recorded in New England, compare it to other small yellow wildflowers in the aster family like goldenrods or wild sunflowers. However, none of these relatives produce the distinctive sticky, resinous coating that makes tarweed feel like you've touched fresh tree sap. The compact flower clusters and extremely gummy texture set it apart from all other yellow wildflowers in the region.
